title: No One Is Too Senior to Be Wrong
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece tackles close-mindedness in leadership, arguing that even well-intentioned leaders are vulnerable to moments of rigid thinking, especially when they feel powerful or senior. Rather than relying on willpower alone, it recommends a concrete habit: surveying the opinions of others before announcing your own, precisely at moments when you least want to hear dissent. The article stresses that this isn't just about soliciting a token counterpoint — it means actively seeking out every stakeholder's view, which slows the rush to judgment and exposes flaws in a preferred position. The takeaway is that humility toward being wrong isn't a fixed trait but a discipline that can be built into a repeatable practice.
points: Close-mindedness correlates with feelings of power or status, even among generally open leaders.
A concrete antidote: ask for others' opinions before revealing your own, especially when you'd rather not.
The rule works best when it means surveying every stakeholder, not just token dissent.
Seeking outside views slows internal judgment and exposes flaws in a preferred position.
Guarding against rigidity is framed as a repeatable discipline, not a personality trait.
quotes: Everyone agrees that close-mindedness is a disease that undermines effective leadership.
The quality of their decisions can be found at the dollar store.
The likelihood of shutting the mind is highly correlated with a feeling of power or status in a given moment.
Asking others to state their opinion slows down the internal thinking process and softens the commitment to any particular view.
They believe adherence to this rule prevents them from raising the drawbridge and hunkering down behind the walls of self-protection.
